chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Hamza ibn Muhammad, who said:
I wrote to Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) asking him about the body and the image. So he wrote back: Glorified is the One like Whom there is nothing — neither a body nor an image.
And it was also narrated by Muhammad ibn Abi Abdillah, except that he did not name the man.

key_terms.الصُّورَةُ: surah — form, image, shape; the attribution of a visible form or image to God
key_terms.الْجِسْمُ: jism — body, corporeality, material substance; in theology, refers to the anthropomorphic attribution of a physical body to God
key_terms.سُبْحَانَ: subhan — glorified/exalted is; a formula of divine transcendence and praise
key_terms.كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ: nothing like His likeness; a direct citation of Quran 42:11 establishing God's radical otherness

ai.seo_question: Does God have a body or image according to Shia Islam?
ai.summary: Hamza ibn Muhammad wrote to Imam al-Ridha (peace be upon him) — referred to by his kunya Abu al-Hasan — asking a theological question about whether God can be described with a body (jism) or an image/form (surah). The Imam responded in writing by citing the Quranic phrase from Surah al-Shura (42:11), 'there is nothing like His likeness,' and then explicitly negating both attributes: neither body nor form. This hadith establishes the foundational Shia theological position of tanzih (divine transcendence from anthropomorphism), affirming that God is wholly unlike created things in every possible physical dimension.
word_analysis: and it was also narrated by him
